rules.statement: In production code, an async method returns ValueTask/ValueTask<T>, ends in `Async`, and takes a CancellationToken as its last parameter, even when none of its awaited calls accepts one; a root call site with no token passes CancellationToken.None.
rules.why: The token is part of the method's contract, so a call added later honors it.
rules.check: Look for own async methods returning Task/Task<T> or lacking a trailing CancellationToken (framework-boundary contracts such as mediator handlers, overrides of foreign members, middleware Invoke and xUnit tests are exempt).

rules.statement: In production code, a method whose work must not be dropped by a caller's abort (post-commit work on its own bounded token, or work an ADR makes uncancellable on CancellationToken.None) takes no CancellationToken parameter and carries a `[SuppressMessage("Design", "NCID0003", Justification = ...)]` whose justification cites the ADR; don't report such a method for lacking a token.
rules.why: A token parameter it ignores would misstate its cancellation, and a caller-passed token could drop the effect.
rules.check: For an async method without a trailing token, check for a suppression citing an ADR; flag a suppression without an ADR citation, or an ignored token parameter on such a method.

rules.statement: In production code, never block on async work (sync-over-async such as .Result, .Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()).
rules.why: Banned in every project via BannedSymbols.
rules.check: Look for blocking waits on tasks.

rules.statement: In production code, offload fire-and-forget work with Task.Run, never Task.Factory.StartNew with an async delegate.
rules.why: StartNew with an async delegate returns a Task<Task> that does not represent the work.
rules.check: Look for Task.Factory.StartNew given an async lambda.

rules.statement: In production code, do not use ConfigureAwait(false); the libraries are ASP.NET Core-oriented and CA2007 is disabled rather than required.
rules.why: Under ASP.NET Core there is no synchronization context, so the call is noise.
rules.check: Look for ConfigureAwait(false) calls, and don't ask for them to be added.

rules.statement: In production code, treat an OperationCanceledException caused by request abort as a client disconnect, not an error to log or answer as a failure.
rules.why: A request abort is a disconnect, not a server fault.
rules.check: Look for catch blocks or handlers that log request-aborted cancellation as an error or return a 500.

rules.statement: In production code, a form body that cannot be read (ReadFormAsync throws InvalidDataException for a malformed body or one over the limits) is answered as a client error (400 invalid_request), read once up front, before client authentication, through the single shared try-read helper, never a local copy.
rules.why: Unhandled, the exception becomes a 500; one shared reader keeps every endpoint consistent, and later readers get the cached form.
rules.check: Look for direct ReadFormAsync calls, duplicated try-read-form helpers, or form reads after client authentication.

rules.statement: In production code, a background loop treats an OperationCanceledException as a failure unless its own stopping token is cancelled.
rules.why: A cancellation from some other token is a failure of the work, not shutdown.
rules.check: Look for catch (OperationCanceledException) in worker loops that don't check the stopping token's IsCancellationRequested (e.g. via a `when` filter).

rules.statement: In production code, use collection expressions, `const` for compile-time literals, and `u8` UTF-8 literals, with a fixed protocol label (an HKDF info or hash prefix) exposed as a `static ReadOnlySpan<byte>` property.
rules.why: Template conventions enforced by analyzers.
rules.check: Look for older collection initializers, non-const literal fields, and byte arrays built for fixed labels.

rules.statement: In production code, nullable reference types are on with warnings as errors, and the null-forgiving operator `!` is banned.
rules.why: Template nullability rule.
rules.check: Look for `!` null-forgiving usage.

rules.statement: In production code, don't treat `T?` under a `where T : notnull` constraint as Nullable<T> for a value type; it is only an annotation, and a value-type T gets no HasValue/null state.
rules.why: This bit the settings lattice.
rules.check: Look for generic code with `where T : notnull` that uses `T?` expecting null to represent 'unset' for value types.

rules.statement: In production code, use Debug.Assert only for internal invariants, never to validate input.
rules.why: Asserts vanish in release builds.
rules.check: Look for Debug.Assert on parameters or external data.

rules.statement: In production code, validate untrusted text as written, not only as parsed, and never normalize an identifier compared byte for byte (such as a redirect URI) through UriBuilder or a URI JSON converter.
rules.why: Parsing normalizes away differences that exact matching depends on.
rules.check: Look for validation done only on a parsed Uri, or for exact-match identifiers round-tripped through Uri/UriBuilder.

rules.statement: In production code, use auto-properties instead of fields, including private members and a Lock, except const, ref, volatile, fixed-buffer, StructLayout/InlineArray struct fields, or fields used by reference.
rules.why: Enforced by the repository analyzer NCID0001.
rules.check: Look for plain fields outside the exempt categories.

rules.statement: In production code, give each property the narrowest accessor shape it needs (get-only or init over set; private set over public).
rules.why: Template members rule.
rules.check: Look for setters wider than any caller uses.

rules.statement: In production code, use a primary constructor wherever it can express the type, converting single-purpose constructors too; buffering a collection with `[.. param]` or a guard folded into an initializer still fits.
rules.why: Template members rule.
rules.check: Look for explicit constructors that only assign parameters, copy collections or guard arguments.

rules.statement: In production code, place constants and statics at the top of the type; in a static class with C# 14 `extension(...)` blocks, every const, static field, static property and static method (private helpers included) sits before the first extension block.
rules.why: The extension blocks are the class's instance members.
rules.check: Look for static members declared after or between extension blocks or instance members.

rules.statement: In production code, make a type `public` only by deliberate decision; the DefaultFoo implementation behind a public interface stays `internal`.
rules.why: Public surface is a contract.
rules.check: Look for new public types, especially Default* implementations of public interfaces.

rules.statement: In production code, no public API may disable issuer, audience, signature, lifetime or algorithm validation.
rules.why: APIs are correct by default.
rules.check: Look for options or parameters that turn off token validation checks.

rules.statement: In production code, a policy that a replaceable public service must apply is itself a public seam (interface) that a replacement can resolve, not internal logic.
rules.why: Otherwise a replacement cannot apply the same policy.
rules.check: Look for a public replaceable service whose required policy lives in internal helpers.

rules.statement: In production code, validate a token the server itself issued (access token, ID token, id_token_hint) only through the single issued-token validator seam, never through hand-built JWT validation parameters; callers add only the audiences and decryption keys they own.
rules.why: Hand-built copies led introspection to report ID tokens as active access tokens and to ignore revoked sessions.
rules.check: Look for new construction of JWT validation parameters for self-issued tokens.

rules.statement: In production code, restrict a class of caller to some endpoints with opt-in endpoint metadata that fails closed, so a request with no endpoint (such as background work) gets no access.
rules.why: Fail-closed security defaults.
rules.check: Look for endpoint restrictions that default to allow when metadata or endpoint is absent.

rules.statement: In production code, keep CORS off a front-channel (user-agent navigated) endpoint with a marker metadata that the CORS middleware is branched around, never with DisableCors()/DisableCorsAttribute or any other ICorsMetadata.
rules.why: The endpoint middleware throws for an endpoint carrying CORS metadata when no CORS middleware ran, failing every request on a production host without CORS.
rules.check: Look for DisableCors, DisableCorsAttribute or ICorsMetadata on endpoints.

rules.statement: In production code, model a set of named values (kinds, types, modes, scopes, formats, methods, reasons, statuses) as open: `public const string` names in a static class, compared ordinally and documented as the known values, or as registered descriptors or strategies from DI resolved by name through a catalog.
rules.why: The family must be extensible by consumers and sibling packages without editing it.
rules.check: Look for new enums or closed lists representing vocabularies, non-ordinal comparisons, or docs claiming the names are exhaustive.

rules.statement: In production code, allow an enum only when its members are fixed by something that can't grow without this library changing (a fully implemented finite external spec enumeration, the outcome set of one library-owned operation, or a mirror of a framework type), no other package could reasonably need another member, and a new member would require a library change anyway.
rules.why: A scope enum judged closed because the library owned all its entities shut out every extension.
rules.check: For each new enum, ask 'could a package that is not this one ever need to add a member?'.

rules.statement: In production code, don't use [Flags] for a vocabulary that may grow.
rules.why: Its bit space and the meaning of every combination are closed.
rules.check: Look for [Flags] enums representing extensible vocabularies.

rules.statement: In production code, don't encode a vocabulary's hierarchy, compatibility or order in code (a switch, bit mask or hard-coded chain); make it registered data the catalog derives.
rules.why: Hard-coded relationships are lock-in even when names are strings.
rules.check: Look for switches or chains describing relationships between vocabulary members.

rules.statement: In production code, don't choose behavior with an exhaustive switch over an open vocabulary; dispatch to the strategy registered for the name.
rules.why: Extensions cannot add cases to a switch.
rules.check: Look for switch statements over vocabulary names that select behavior.

rules.statement: In production code, don't infer a trait from a vocabulary member's name (such as `EndsWith(".jwt")`); have the registered strategy declare the trait.
rules.why: A suffix or prefix test is a hard-coded relationship.
rules.check: Look for StartsWith/EndsWith/Contains tests on vocabulary names.

rules.statement: In production code, persist or send a vocabulary value as its string name, never an ordinal.
rules.why: An older node that meets a newer member then fails closed by name instead of misreading a number.
rules.check: Look for enums serialized as numbers in storage or on the wire.

rules.statement: In production code, reject input that names an unregistered vocabulary member, never ignore it, and have the catalog validate the whole registered set when it's composed (duplicate names, dangling references, cycles).
rules.why: The vocabulary of registered values is closed.
rules.check: Look for lookups that skip unknown names silently, or catalogs without composition-time validation.

rules.statement: In production code, never expose secret material on the public surface.
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for public properties or methods returning raw key bytes or secrets.

rules.statement: In production code, data, options, context and event types are `sealed`, with init or get-only members and concrete collection types (List<T>, never IList<T>).
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for unsealed DTO/options/event types, settable members, or interface-typed collection properties on them.

rules.statement: In production code, seal a type by derivation intent, not by visibility; abstractions meant as extension points stay unsealed.
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for intended base types being sealed, or types sealed merely because they are internal or public.

rules.statement: In production code, use a `readonly record struct` for a small immutable value (keys, descriptors, command and disposition values).
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for small immutable values modeled as classes or mutable structs.

rules.statement: In production code, a JSON-deserialized DTO captures unknown fields with a `[JsonExtensionData] public Dictionary<string, JsonElement>? ExtensionData { get; set; }` member.
rules.why: An unrecognized wire member round-trips instead of being silently dropped.
rules.check: Look for deserialized DTOs lacking a JsonExtensionData member.

rules.statement: In production code, write a payload persisted at rest as a schema-versioned envelope through the shared persisted-payload serializer, not a bare JsonSerializer call, with no member names beginning with `$`; a payload rewritten in place carries a [JsonExtensionData] bag.
rules.why: Stored documents must be versioned and additive, and a read-modify-write must not drop members it doesn't model.
rules.check: Look for direct JsonSerializer use on stored payloads, `$`-prefixed members, or in-place-updated payloads without extension data.

rules.statement: In production code, a reader of a stored document that lacks the envelope or a member the serving code always writes throws as malformed rather than supplying a default or fallback; such members are `required`, and a non-additive change bumps the payload version and ships one single-step upcaster.
rules.why: Stored data missing written members fails closed.
rules.check: Look for readers defaulting missing stored members, always-written members not marked required, or schema changes without a version bump and upcaster.

rules.statement: In production code, buffer data by default and stream only deliberately.
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for streaming APIs or IAsyncEnumerable introduced without a stated need.

rules.statement: In production code, own every stored collection by copying it rather than keeping a caller's instance, and pick its concrete type by usage.
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for constructors or setters storing a passed-in collection reference directly.

rules.statement: In production code, method signatures use read-only collection interfaces while storage stays concrete, and a local stays concrete through `var` over an explicit initializer.
rules.why: Template types rule.
rules.check: Look for parameters/returns typed as mutable concrete collections, or fields/locals typed as interfaces.

rules.statement: In production code, don't add boolean or flag arguments that select a method's behavior.
rules.why: Template public API rule.
rules.check: Look for bool parameters that switch between code paths.

rules.statement: In production code, a configuration callback takes one growable type (an options or builder object), not multiple positional arguments.
rules.why: Template public API rule; the callback can grow without breaking.
rules.check: Look for Action<...> configuration delegates with multiple parameters.

rules.statement: In production code, don't use cross-assembly InternalsVisibleTo.
rules.why: Template public API rule and ADR.
rules.check: Look for InternalsVisibleTo attributes or csproj items naming production assemblies.

rules.statement: In production code, an implementation package references only *.Abstractions packages (and foundation packages), never another implementation package; cross-implementation collaboration goes through an abstraction interface resolved from DI, with the concrete type referenced only in the composition root.
rules.why: A capability shared by more than one implementation ships as an abstraction/implementation pair.
rules.check: Look for ProjectReference entries in an implementation csproj naming a non-Abstractions, non-foundation package.

rules.statement: In production code, mark an infrastructure-only public type with the summary "This API supports the ... infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code."
rules.why: Template public API rule.
rules.check: Look for public types meant only for infrastructure that lack the summary.

rules.statement: In production code, record every public API change in the sibling PublicAPI.Shipped/Unshipped.txt: remove stale entries by hand after `dotnet format analyzers`, add both the `extension(Receiver!)` container line and the member line for a C# 14 extension member, and keep the files LF.
rules.why: The public surface is tracked; the formatter doesn't reliably remove stale entries and may rewrite the files with CRLF; a breaking change is a major bump.
rules.check: Look for public changes without PublicAPI entries, stale entries, missing extension container lines, or CRLF rewrites of the whole file.

rules.statement: In production code, at most one overload per method name carries optional parameters.
rules.why: RS0026; still rolling out, so it is confirmed in review.
rules.check: Look for multiple overloads of a name each with optional parameters.

rules.statement: In production code, required inputs are constructor parameters, optional inputs are `init` properties, and an evolving set of optional selection criteria is an init-only DTO rather than positional parameters.
rules.why: Template public API rule; DTOs grow without breaking callers.
rules.check: Look for optional inputs as constructor parameters, or filter/query methods with many optional positional parameters.

rules.statement: In production code, annotate a public type consumed by reflection, DI, the options binder or a serializer with JetBrains `[PublicAPI]`, and never apply `[PublicAPI]` to an internal type.
rules.why: It states intent and silences unused-member noise for public types; on internal types it misstates them as public surface.
rules.check: Look for serializer/DI-consumed public types without [PublicAPI], or [PublicAPI] on internal types.

rules.statement: In production code, keep one type per file.
rules.why: Template organization rule.
rules.check: Look for files declaring multiple top-level types.

rules.statement: In production code, name the single canonical implementation of an `IFoo` `DefaultFoo`.
rules.why: Template organization rule and ADR.
rules.check: Look for canonical implementations named otherwise (FooService, FooImpl).

rules.statement: In production code, don't declare nested types, except the template's two allowed cases.
rules.why: Template organization rule.
rules.check: Look for types declared inside other types.

rules.statement: In production code, place a type in a folder named for its purpose; a contract, its DTOs and its Default implementation share one purpose namespace across the abstractions/implementation pair, that folder registers its own services, and a service used by a single feature lives with that feature.
rules.why: Template organization rule; types are organized by purpose.
rules.check: Look for types grouped by kind (Interfaces/, Models/) or scattered away from their contract.

rules.statement: In production code, don't report a public namespace that doesn't mirror its folder; the namespace is a stable contract (IDE0130 is off), except that public options in an `Options/` folder carry a `.Options` sub-namespace.
rules.why: The public namespace is a stable contract pinned by RootNamespace.
rules.check: Before flagging a namespace/folder mismatch, check whether the type is public options (which should use .Options).

rules.statement: In production code, an interface name states the role and leaves the brand to the namespace (no product prefix in the type name).
rules.why: Template organization rule.
rules.check: Look for interface names prefixed with the product or brand name.
